items.q: In an LRU cache built from a hash table plus a doubly-linked list, what is each structure's job?

options.t: The table finds any entry in O(1); the list orders entries by recency so eviction pops the tail
options.why: Right — both structures point at the same entry objects. Lookup never scans, and eviction never searches: a GET is one hash lookup plus two pointer splices to move the entry to the head.

options.t: The hash table stores keys, the list stores values
options.why: Keys and values live together in one entry object. The two structures are two different ways of reaching that same object — by name, and by recency.

options.t: The list chains entries that collide in the same hash bucket, so lookups stay fast as the table fills
options.why: The recency list has nothing to do with collision handling. Its only job is ordering entries by last use so the coldest one is always at the tail.

options.t: The hash table handles reads and the list handles writes
options.why: Both reads and writes touch both structures: any access looks up via the table and then re-links the entry to the list head.

items.q: Why must the recency list be doubly linked rather than singly linked?

options.t: Removing a mid-list entry needs its predecessor — a back-pointer gives it in O(1)
options.why: Exactly. Every GET unlinks an entry from mid-list to move it to the head. With billions of entries, an O(n) walk per access is dead on arrival.

options.t: Doubly-linked lists use less memory
options.why: The opposite — the extra back-pointer costs 8 bytes per entry. You pay that memory precisely to buy O(1) mid-list removal.

options.t: Singly-linked lists can't be iterated
options.why: They iterate fine, forward. Iteration isn't the issue — surgically removing a node from the middle without walking is.

options.t: It makes the list thread-safe
options.why: Pointer direction has nothing to do with thread safety — a doubly-linked list under concurrency still needs a lock or sharding. That contention is one reason real caches approximate LRU instead.

items.q: A cache uses only lazy expiry (check TTL on read). What problem does the active sampler solve?

options.t: Expired keys nobody reads again squat in memory until eviction stumbles on them
options.why: Right. Lazy expiry only fires on access. The sampler (Redis's version: 20 random TTL keys, 10x/sec, loop while >25% are expired) reclaims dead keys nobody will ever touch.

options.t: Without it, a read could hand back a value whose TTL passed hours ago, so lazy checking alone is unsafe
options.why: No — lazy expiry is correct: the read checks the timestamp and treats an expired entry as a miss. The problem is memory, not correctness.

options.t: It makes TTLs more precise
options.why: Expiry precision is already exact at read time under lazy checking. The sampler is about reclaiming memory from keys that will never be read.

options.t: It reduces read latency
options.why: The timestamp check on read costs nanoseconds either way. The sampler trades a little background CPU for reclaimed memory — latency is unchanged.

items.q: A 56-node cluster adds one node. Roughly what fraction of keys change owner with consistent hashing, versus hash(key) mod N?

options.t: About 1/57 with the ring; about 98% with mod N
options.why: Right — the ring moves only K/N keys (the arcs the new node claims); mod N re-addresses nearly every key because the divisor changed. That difference is a ripple versus a cluster-wide cold start.

options.t: About half in both cases
options.why: Neither. The whole point of consistent hashing is that membership change moves only ~K/N keys — a couple of percent here, not half.

options.t: About 1/57 in both cases
options.why: Mod N isn't that gentle: a key keeps its slot only if hash mod 56 equals hash mod 57, which almost never holds. Roughly 98% of keys move.

options.t: Zero with the ring — existing keys never move
options.why: The new node has to own something, so the keys in its claimed arcs do move. 'Small and bounded', not 'zero', is the ring's promise.

items.q: Why does each physical node appear at ~200 positions on the ring instead of one?

options.t: They average arc sizes for even load, and a dead node's ranges scatter across survivors
options.why: Both halves matter: 200 samples per node tightens load spread to a few percent, and failure dumps 200 crumbs onto many nodes instead of one boulder onto a single neighbor.

options.t: It increases total cache capacity
options.why: Vnodes are just extra ring positions — pointers, not memory. Capacity is set by RAM, and 200 vnodes add none.

options.t: It makes key lookups faster
options.why: Slightly the opposite — more ring entries mean a marginally bigger binary search. You pay that tiny cost to buy even load and gentle failure.

options.t: Each key lands on several vnode positions, which is how the cluster keeps redundant copies
options.why: Vnodes are 200 addresses for the same physical machine — copies of the node's ring presence, not of any data. Replication is a separate primary-to-replica stream.

items.q: In this design, what is the primary purpose of each shard's replica?

options.t: Protecting hit rate and latency when the primary dies — not durability
options.why: Right. The database is the source of truth; nothing in the cache needs to survive. The replica exists so a primary failure doesn't turn 1/56th of the working set into a database stampede.

options.t: Guaranteeing no acknowledged write is ever lost
options.why: That's a database's promise. Replication here is async with no acknowledgment — a dying primary can lose its last few milliseconds of writes, and that's fine: loss = misses.

options.t: Serving all reads while the primary serves writes, so read and write load never compete
options.why: By default reads go to the primary (freshest data, one hop). Replica reads are an opt-in (STALE_OK) used for hot keys, not the standard path.

options.t: Storing a second copy in case of disk failure
options.why: There are no disks in the hot design — it's an in-memory cache. The replica guards against process and machine loss, for hit-rate reasons.

items.q: A client sends GET to a node and receives MOVED shard=9 epoch=14. What happened?

options.t: The client's map is stale — refresh topology and retry against the new owner
options.why: Right — MOVED is a redirect plus a nudge. The epoch tells the client its map (say, epoch 13) is behind; one config fetch and one retry later, the app never sees an error.

options.t: The key was evicted and must be re-fetched from the database
options.why: That would be a plain MISS. MOVED says nothing about the key's presence — it says you asked the wrong node.

options.t: The cluster lost quorum on its topology and is rejecting traffic until membership settles
options.why: MOVED is routine, not an emergency — it's exactly how requests keep succeeding during rebalances and failovers, at the cost of one extra round trip.

options.t: The node is overloaded and shedding load
options.why: Load shedding would be a busy/throttle signal. MOVED is about ownership: this key's slot now belongs to another node, per a newer epoch.

items.q: What is a lease, in the Facebook memcache sense?

options.t: A token given to the first client that misses; only a SET carrying it is accepted
options.why: Right — one mechanism, two kills: the miss stampede collapses to one database query, and a DEL invalidating the token stops a slow reader from writing stale data back.

options.t: A time-limited lock a client takes before any read
options.why: Locking every read would put a coordination step on the hot path. Leases only appear on a miss — the slow path — where coordination pays for itself.

options.t: A reservation of memory for a key before its value arrives
options.why: No memory is reserved. The lease is a small token binding 'whoever is refilling this key' to the eventual SET.

options.t: A subscription that pushes every value change out to clients so their copies stay fresh
options.why: That's an invalidation/pub-sub channel — a different mechanism. Leases coordinate who refills a missing key, not who hears about changes.

items.q: What's the difference between allkeys-LRU and volatile-LRU eviction?

options.t: allkeys may evict any key; volatile evicts only keys that carry a TTL
options.why: Right. Pure caches run allkeys — everything is refetchable. Volatile suits mixed workloads where some keys (no TTL) must never silently vanish under memory pressure.

options.t: allkeys is exact LRU; volatile is approximate
options.why: Both are typically sampled/approximate. The policies differ in which keys are eligible for eviction, not in how recency is tracked.

options.t: volatile evicts keys the moment they expire; allkeys waits for pressure
options.why: Expiry and eviction are different machines. Expiry removes keys past their TTL regardless of pressure; eviction picks victims under memory pressure — volatile just restricts the victim pool to TTL-carrying keys.

options.t: They're two names for the same policy
options.why: They differ exactly when a no-TTL key exists under memory pressure: allkeys can evict it, volatile cannot — which can mean volatile runs out of victims and must refuse writes.

items.q: A 56-primary cluster at 95% hit rate loses one primary that has no replica. The database normally sees 100K reads/sec. What happens next?

options.t: About 34K extra reads/sec hit the database — a +34% spike, instantly
options.why: Right: ~1.8% of the working set went dark, and its reads (about 1.7% of 2M/sec) become misses. This math is why replicas exist and why the database needs N−1 headroom.

options.t: Hit rate falls about 2%, which the remaining nodes absorb
options.why: The hit rate drop is small, but the other cache nodes can't absorb it — misses go to the database, and a +34% sudden spike on the DB is the actual risk.

options.t: The other 55 primaries take over its keys automatically with data intact
options.why: The ring reassigns ownership of the key ranges, but the data in RAM died with the node. New owners start cold for those keys — that's exactly the miss storm.

options.t: Nothing significant — caches are designed to lose nodes
options.why: The cache is fine; the database is the concern. 'Designed to lose nodes' only holds if the DB was provisioned for the resulting miss storm — that's the N−1 rule.

items.q: Reader R misses, reads v1 from the DB, then stalls in a GC pause. Writer W updates the DB to v2 and DELs the cache key. R wakes and SETs v1. Which mechanism prevents the cache serving stale v1 until TTL?

options.t: Leases or versioned SETs — the cache refuses R's late write
options.why: Right — this is the read-modify race, and the fix is making the cache refuse writes that lost the race: an invalidated lease token or a version regression check at SET time.

options.t: Shorter TTLs on hot keys
options.why: TTL only bounds how long the wrong value survives; it doesn't stop it being written. You'd still serve stale data for the whole TTL window — a mitigation, not a fix.

options.t: Having W write v2 into the cache instead of deleting the key, so a fresh value is always present
options.why: Set-on-write makes it worse: now W's v2 SET and R's v1 SET race directly, and network reordering decides who wins. Without versions, last-writer-wins is decided by luck.

options.t: Retrying the DEL a few times
options.why: The DEL succeeded! It just happened before R's stale SET arrived. No amount of DEL retries fixes an ordering problem — refusing the stale write does.

items.q: Your top-N sketch shows one key taking 500K reads/sec against a primary sized for 36K. First mitigation to reach for?

options.t: A tiny client-side L1 cache with ~1s TTL for detected hot keys
options.why: Right — it collapses per-key load to at most one refresh per app server per second, costs almost nothing, bounds staleness at 1s, and requires no cluster change. Cheapest lever first.

options.t: Reshard the cluster to spread the key
options.why: One key hashes to one place no matter how many shards exist — resharding moves the hot spot, it doesn't split it. A single hot key is a routing/edge problem, not a capacity problem.

options.t: Move that shard to a bigger machine
options.why: A vertical band-aid: 14x over capacity today, and the next viral key lands wherever it hashes. You'd be buying hardware to chase a routing problem.

options.t: Rate-limit reads for that key
options.why: Throttling your own cache turns a hot key into user-visible errors or DB load. The load is legitimate; serve it cheaply at the edge instead of refusing it.

items.q: After a deploy that changed object serialization, hit rate drops 14 points. Traffic flat, nodes healthy, TTLs unchanged, evictions/sec tripled, boxes show free-ish memory locked in unused size classes. Diagnosis?

options.t: Slab calcification — pages stuck in old size classes starve the new sizes
options.why: Right — Twitter's exact incident. The value-size distribution shifted, the allocator's page assignments didn't. Fix: slab page rebalancing (Twemcache's random slab eviction) or a careful replica-promote roll to reset allocator state.

options.t: The working set quietly outgrew the cluster's RAM, so entries now evict each other
options.why: Growth would show as gradually rising evictions with rising traffic — not a step change on deploy day with memory idle in the wrong size classes. Ask 'what changed?' before buying nodes.

options.t: The active TTL sampler is deleting too aggressively
options.why: The sampler only removes already-expired keys, and TTLs didn't change. Tripled evictions (not expirations) point at memory pressure, not expiry.

options.t: Hash collisions increased because keys changed
options.why: Collisions degrade lookup speed marginally; they don't evict anything or cause misses. The eviction spike plus stranded slab memory is the tell.

items.q: The p99 budget is 1ms in-datacenter, where one network round trip costs 100–500µs. What does this imply for routing?

options.t: Route clients straight to the owning node — a proxy hop eats the budget
options.why: Right — the lookup is ~1µs; the network IS the latency. Adding a proxy roughly doubles the wire time, so the ring must live in the client. Estimation gating an architecture choice.

options.t: Use a proxy tier so routing logic stays centralized
options.why: Centralized routing is a real benefit (Facebook chose it with mcrouter for polyglot-fleet reasons) — but it costs the extra hop this latency budget can't pay. Know which constraint is binding here.

options.t: Co-locate a cache instance on every app server so lookups never touch the network
options.why: Local caches eliminate the hop but shatter the shared working set — each host caches its own copy, slashing effective capacity and hit rate. That's what the small L1 is for, scoped to hot keys only.

options.t: The budget is impossible without kernel bypass
options.why: 300µs round trip + microseconds of processing fits 1ms with room to spare — with one hop. Exotic networking isn't needed; avoiding a second hop is.

items.q: A primary pauses for 20s of GC. The config service promotes its replica at epoch 13. The old primary wakes, still thinking it owns shard 7. What stops it doing damage?

options.t: Epoch fencing — everyone refuses anything stamped epoch 12
options.why: Right. Nobody relies on the zombie realizing it's dead; everyone else just compares numbers. In a cache the damage would only be staleness — but the fence (chapter 2.3) makes even that window tiny.

options.t: The health checker kills the process before it can serve
options.why: You can't count on kill signals reaching a partitioned or paused node in time — that race is exactly why fencing exists. Correctness can't depend on the murder arriving first.

options.t: GC pauses under 30s are within the failover timeout, so this can't happen
options.why: The failover already happened at ~5s of missed heartbeats — a 20s pause sails past it. Designs that assume pauses stay conveniently short meet reality quickly.

options.t: Nothing — but it doesn't matter in a cache
options.why: Half-right instincts, wrong conclusion: unfenced split-brain means two nodes accepting writes for the same keys indefinitely, and clients ping-ponging between fresh and stale. Cheap insurance (an integer compare) buys it off.

items.q: You need to roll a new cache binary to all 112 nodes. What's the right deploy dance?

options.t: Per shard: warm a new-version replica from the stream, then promote it by epoch bump
options.why: Right — the fleet upgrades with hit rate intact, one epoch at a time, and you watch per-shard hit rate between steps. A cache's memory is its value; a deploy must never empty it.

options.t: Rolling restart, one node at a time, like any stateless service
options.why: A cache isn't stateless — restart discards RAM. Rolling through 112 nodes is 112 sequential cold shards, hours of elevated DB load. 'Like any service' is the trap phrase.

options.t: Restart everything at 3am during low traffic
options.why: A fully cold cluster at 40% hit rate can overwhelm the DB even at overnight traffic — and you've bet the site on nothing else going wrong before it warms. Blast radius, not clock time, is the knob.

options.t: Snapshot each node's memory to disk, restart on the new binary, then reload the snapshot
options.why: Workable (Redis persists this way) but we deliberately built no persistence — and snapshot-reload adds minutes of staleness and disk machinery for what replica-promote does warm and live.

items.q: A popular key expires and 1,000 servers miss within 50ms. With leases plus STALE_OK, what does the database experience?

options.t: One query — the lease holder refills, everyone else waits or takes stale
options.why: Right — that's the coalescing contract, and it's the documented effect in Facebook's paper (one experiment: peak DB queries fell from ~17K/s to ~1.3K/s with leases on).

options.t: 1,000 queries, but spread over a few seconds
options.why: That's what jittered retries alone would buy you — smearing the stampede, not shrinking it. Leases change the count, not just the shape.

options.t: Zero queries — stale data is served until the next natural write
options.why: Someone must still refresh the value — the lease holder does, once. Serving stale forever with no refill path isn't a cache, it's a rumor mill.

options.t: One query per cache node that holds the key
options.why: A key lives on one shard (plus replica) — and coalescing happens at that owner, so it's one query total, not per-node.

items.q: 30 TB database, top 10% of data serves ~93% of reads, 2M GETs/sec peak, 128 GB nodes budgeting 64 GB of entries each. What sets the primary count, and roughly what is it?

options.t: Memory: 3.3 TB / 64 GB ≈ 52 → ~56 primaries; CPU would be loafing
options.why: Right — and saying 'RAM sets the count, cores will be bored' is the estimation-driving-design moment. Throughput per node lands far below what an event loop handles.

options.t: CPU: 2M ops/sec at 100K per node ≈ 20 primaries, then round up for headroom
options.why: 20 nodes × 64 GB is 1.3 TB — less than half the working set fits, and hit rate collapses. When both constraints exist, the binding one (memory) wins.

options.t: You need to cache all 30 TB, so ~470 primaries
options.why: Caching everything ignores the skew that makes caching economical — the cold 90% of data would occupy RAM to serve 7% of reads. Working set, not dataset, sizes a cache.

options.t: Network bandwidth per node
options.why: 36K ops/sec × ~1 KB ≈ 36 MB/s — a few percent of a modern NIC. Bandwidth matters for value-heavy workloads, but the numbers here say RAM binds first.

items.q: Interviewer: 'Your replication can lose acknowledged writes. Why not make it synchronous?' The senior answer:

options.t: "It's a cache — a lost write is a miss the DB self-heals. Sync doubles write latency for nothing."
options.why: Right — the failure model does the arguing. Matching guarantees to actual requirements, and naming what you deliberately gave up, is the judgment being probed.

options.t: "Good point — I'd make replication synchronous to be safe."
options.why: Folding under a probe reads worse than the original choice. 'To be safe' buys nothing here (the DB already holds truth) and silently spends your p99 — that's cost without benefit.

options.t: "I'd make replication configurable — sync or async per keyspace — so each team picks the guarantee that suits their data."
options.why: Configurability as a dodge — you now maintain two consistency modes, and the question ('what does THIS system need?') is still unanswered. Commit, then bend only for a named requirement.

options.t: "Async is what Redis does, so it's the industry standard."
options.why: Appeal to authority instead of reasoning. Redis async replication exists for reasons — say the reasons. 'X does it' collapses under one follow-up: 'why does X do it?'

items.q: In 'build a distributed cache', where should a senior candidate spend the deepest 10 minutes?

options.t: Cluster behavior under change — rebalancing, epochs, fenced failover
options.why: That's the fire. A static cluster is easy and a single node is well-trodden; the traps interviewers hold in reserve (zombie primaries, stale maps, in-flight ops during migration) all live in the transitions.

options.t: The LRU implementation — the O(1) hash-table-plus-list dance is the algorithmic heart of it
options.why: It's a classic warm-up (know the O(1) dance cold), but it's also on every study list — depth there differentiates nobody at the senior bar. Ten minutes on pointers is ten minutes not spent on the hard part.

options.t: Choosing the fastest hash function
options.why: Any modern non-cryptographic hash disappears into the noise next to a 300µs network hop. This is bikeshedding dressed as rigor.

options.t: The wire protocol design
options.why: Worth two committed minutes (framing, pipelining, the lease/version flags) — the flags matter, the byte layout doesn't. The protocol serves the deep dives; it isn't one.

items.q: The interviewer 10x's everything: 33 TB working set, 6M GETs/sec. What breaks first in the committed design?

options.t: The smart client's connection fan-out — millions of sockets; time for a per-host sidecar proxy
options.why: Right — and the senior tell is naming which committed choice stops paying (direct connections) and evolving it, while noting the epoch/ring protocol survives 10x untouched.

options.t: The consistent hashing ring stops scaling once it holds six figures of vnode entries and lookups slow
options.why: The ring is a sorted array of ~112K entries with binary search — nanoseconds. Topology metadata scales logarithmically in effort; it's the last thing to break.

options.t: The config service becomes the bottleneck
options.why: It's off the data path and its state is tiny; it publishes maps on change, not per request. 10x traffic doesn't touch it — this answer confuses control plane with data plane.

options.t: Nothing — the design scales horizontally
options.why: 'Horizontally scalable' as an incantation is the buzzword shield from chapter 0.1. Every design has a next wall; claiming otherwise tells the interviewer you haven't looked for yours.

items.q: Requirement flip: 'after a DB write, no cached read may be more than 1 second stale.' The strongest response:

options.t: "Cache-aside can't promise it. I'd add versioned SETs plus CDC invalidation with lag as an SLO, scoped to that keyspace."
options.why: Names the honest limit, the mechanism, the new dependency's cost, and scopes the guarantee instead of re-architecting everything — including questioning the requirement. That's the full senior package.

options.t: "Set TTLs to 1 second on everything."
options.why: This nukes the hit rate — every key now refetches every second whether it changed or not — and still doesn't bound staleness from the race conditions. It confuses expiry with invalidation.

options.t: "I'd make every write path write-through to the cache synchronously, inside the same transaction as the database write, so the two can never diverge."
options.why: Closer, but without versioning the write-write races reappear, every write path in the company must now participate correctly, and DB transactions + cache writes can't be made atomic — the gap this 'fix' pretends away.

options.t: "Caches are eventually consistent; the requirement is unreasonable."
options.why: Refusing the requirement isn't engineering it. Bounded staleness IS achievable (CDC lag + version guards) — the senior move is pricing it, not denying it.

items.q: A cache node dies and its keys' traffic must go somewhere. Facebook chose a small 'gutter' pool with short TTLs over rehashing the dead node's keys to surviving neighbors. Why?

options.t: Rehashing dumps the dead node's load onto busy survivors and can topple them in turn
options.why: Right — it's cascade prevention. Failure traffic goes to idle, disposable capacity instead of loading the healthy fleet, and expiring fast means the gutter never needs to be invalidation-correct.

options.t: Rehashing would permanently corrupt the ring
options.why: Nothing corrupts — the ring handles reassignment cleanly. The problem is load dynamics on the survivors, not data structure correctness.

options.t: The gutter provides stronger consistency than the main pool
options.why: Weaker, if anything — gutter entries dodge the invalidation machinery entirely, which is why their TTLs are kept short. The trade is deliberate: brief staleness for cascade immunity.

options.t: Gutter machines are cheaper than regular cache machines
options.why: Same hardware — about 1% of the fleet held idle. The insight is where failure traffic lands, not what it costs; you pay for the idle pool precisely so failures have a padded room.

items.q: Interviewer: 'Your sampled eviction isn't true LRU. Make it exact.' The senior response:

options.t: "I'd push back: exact LRU costs a lock on every GET, and sampling already matches its hit rate."
options.why: Quantified pushback beats compliance: name the cost of exactness, the near-zero benefit, and where the budget would actually pay. Redis's own documented design makes this a defensible hill.

options.t: "Sure — one global doubly-linked list with a mutex around it, and I'd shard the lock if it got hot."
options.why: Obedient and wrong: you just serialized every GET on every connection through one lock in a system sized for 100K ops/sec/node. Complying with a bad requirement is not collaboration.

options.t: "Exact LRU is impossible in distributed systems."
options.why: Overclaim — it's entirely possible per node (chapter 1.6 built one); it's just a poor trade at this concurrency and scale. 'Impossible' where the truth is 'expensive and pointless' invites an easy counterexample.

options.t: "I'd switch to LFU instead, it's more accurate."
options.why: A lateral dodge — LFU is a different policy with its own approximations and its own aging problems, not 'more accurate LRU.' The question was about the exactness trade-off; answer that.

items.q: You get one 3am page for this cache. What should trigger it?

options.t: Database read QPS breaching the headroom the cache exists to protect
options.why: Page on the harm, not the mechanism: every cache failure mode (dead node, calcification, stuck epochs, stampede) matters exactly insofar as it drives DB load toward the cliff. Hit rate tells you which shard; DB QPS tells you it's 3am-worthy.

options.t: Any single node going unhealthy
options.why: That's designed-for and self-healing (replica promotes in seconds) — a ticket, not a page. Paging on expected events trains on-call to ignore the pager.

options.t: Evictions/sec exceeding a fixed threshold
options.why: Evictions at steady state are normal cache breathing — a full cache evicts on every insert. The trend against traffic is a capacity warning for daytime review, not a 3am wake-up.

options.t: p99 latency above 1ms on any shard
options.why: Worth alerting during the day, but a brief p99 wobble doesn't threaten the business the way DB saturation does. If the wobble is real trouble, it shows up in the miss path — which the DB QPS page catches.
